# The Unlit Country

In the early morning of January 17, 1994, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake woke Los Angeles, threw the city into darkness, and sent residents stumbling from their homes. Some of them looked up. Some of them, alarmed by what they saw, called 911 to report a vast, strange, silvery cloud hanging over the city. The operators had to explain: that was the Milky Way. The callers had never seen it before. They had lived their entire lives beneath a sky from which their own galaxy had been quietly erased, and when it reappeared they mistook it for an emergency.

I think about those phone calls often. They are funny, in the way true things are funny, and then they are not. More than a third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from home. In Europe the figure is around sixty percent; in North America, nearly eighty. The most rigorous mapping we have — a 2016 atlas assembled from satellite data — found that more than eighty percent of people live under skies measurably brightened by artificial light. In Singapore the night is so bright that residents' eyes never fully complete their adaptation to darkness. There are children in that city who have never seen a star.

We tend to describe this as the loss of a view. That undersells it. What we have been losing is a country — an unlit country that human beings have inhabited for as long as we have been human, a geography of thought and feeling that we dismantled in a few generations without quite noticing it was there.

For nearly all of our history, night was a second country with its own laws. The historian Roger Ekirch, burrowing through court records, diaries, and medical texts, found that before the late seventeenth century people slept in two shifts. There was a first sleep, then a calm interval of wakefulness in the small hours — people prayed, reflected, talked, made love, visited neighbors by moonlight — and then a second sleep until dawn. The night was not an interruption of life. It was a room in the house.

Above that room hung the instruments. The stars were the calendar that told you when to plant, the compass that carried Polynesian navigators across a thousand miles of open ocean, the almanac, the clock, and the cinema — a screen on which every culture projected its gods, its animals, its dead. Escaping north, enslaved people read the sky like a map, the Drinking Gourd swinging its handle toward the pole. The night was not empty. It was infrastructure. It was also, despite all that use, a place of terror and of consolation, the one landscape no one had ever finished looking at.

Darkness itself is not an absence. Biologists know this. Descend past a thousand meters of ocean and you enter the midnight zone, where no sunlight reaches and the only lights left are the ones living things make — lures, flares, burglar alarms of bioluminescence. In the complete dark of caves, animals dismantle their own eyes over generations; the darkness is such a total environment that sight becomes an expense worth cutting. Whole ecosystems run on darkness the way forests run on sunlight. The dark is a habitat. It has residents.

We are learning, rather late, that we had residents too. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the nest at night and crawl toward the brighter horizon, which for a hundred million years meant the sea, starlight lying on water. Now the brighter horizon is often the boardwalk, the highway, the resort, and the hatchlings crawl inland and die there by the tens of thousands. Migrating birds, crossing continents at night by stars and by magnetism, meet a lit tower in the fog and circle it until they drop. Insects spiral into streetlights. We have been running, uncontrolled and largely unexamined, the largest lighting experiment in the history of life, and the results are posted nightly at the base of every glowing tower.

The loss runs inward as well as up. Darkness is not just where the turtles are; it is a condition of the body. Sleep is not a switch but a tide, and it needs the dark to turn. While we lie in it, the brain's waste-clearance system — a plumbing network discovered only in 2012 that rinses the brain with cerebrospinal fluid — does its night work. The pineal gland, a tiny organ Descartes mistook for the seat of the soul, measures the length of the night and tunes our seasons of mood and sleep. When we light the night, we lie to that organ. We tell it, in chemical terms, that the long dark has ended. The body believes us, and suffers.

Here is the strange turn: having abolished the dark almost everywhere, we have begun to tour it. There are certified dark-sky reserves where the Milky Way still shows — Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand, the high desert of the Atacama — and people travel thousands of miles and wait for the moon to wane, all to see the thing that used to be the common property of every creature with eyes lifted from a nest or a savanna or a bed. First-time viewers often go silent. Some cry. The guides who run these trips have come to expect it. What people are weeping for is not exactly the stars. It is the recognition of an enormous thing that had been there the whole time, unseen, patient, overhead, while they lived beneath it and never once looked.

The universe, for its part, remains mostly dark. Ordinary matter — stars, planets, us, everything we can touch — is the thin exception, a foam on a sea of dark matter and darker energy. The dark was never a failure of lighting. It is the default condition of everything, and we spent a few centuries treating it as a defect to be corrected, one lamp at a time.

I don't want to go back to tallow and terror. I like that I can read at night; I like that a dark street is not automatically a danger. But I want the unlit country back as a neighbor, not a ruin. It is still there, barely, at the end of certain roads. The smear those Angelenos reported in 1994 is not a cloud and never was an emergency. It is a hundred billion suns seen edge-on from the inside, a disk a hundred thousand light-years wide, hanging over the parking lot and the highway and the yard wherever the last unlit miles remain. You have to go and stand under it. You have to turn from the lit windows and look up. It has been waiting the whole time, the way dark things wait — without moving, without dimming, without asking to be seen.
